question:
Patient note:
A 56-year-old man sits upright on the stretcher in the ambulatory surgery holding area awaiting a right knee arthroscopy with partial medial meniscectomy that the orthopedic service expects will last less than one hour under general anesthesia; he drove himself to the hospital this morning, ascended the front steps without shortness of breath, and reports that aside from the catching pain in his knee he walks two miles every evening with his dog and climbs a flight of stairs to his second-floor bedroom without assistance, thereby remaining fully active at baseline. He has not been hospitalized or undergone any major operation in recent years, and his only prior exposure to an operating room was a simple inguinal hernia repair performed eight years ago; that episode was complicated by an abrupt platelet fall on postoperative day four, and enzyme-linked immunoassay later demonstrated antibodies against platelet factor 4–heparin complexes, prompting cessation of all heparin products and substitution of a direct thrombin inhibitor until platelet recovery—since that event he carries a wallet card stating that unfractionated and low-molecular-weight heparin should be avoided. He denies ever having clots in the legs or lungs, recalls no episodes of unilateral calf swelling, chest pain, or unexplained dyspnea, and duplex imaging has never been performed for suspicion of venous thromboembolism. Neither leg is in a cast or brace, and he has not experienced fractures, multisystem injuries, neurologic deficits, or spine trauma; his gait is steady, and he continues to work full time as a city building inspector, walking construction sites five days a week. Over the past month there has been no fever, rigors, urinary or biliary infection, bacteremia, or systemic inflammatory response, and he has not been treated for pneumonia or received intravenous antibiotics. He has never been admitted for heart failure, describes no orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and an echocardiogram done two years ago for a benign murmur showed preserved ejection fraction with trivial mitral regurgitation. Respiratory history is notable for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease attributed to a 40-pack-year smoking habit that he quit five years earlier; baseline symptoms consist of morning cough productive of scant clear sputum and occasional exertional wheeze relieved by two puffs of albuterol, and he has not required systemic corticosteroids or hospitalization within the past twelve months. He denies myocardial infarction, inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy, autoimmune conditions, or exposure to long-term steroids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or estrogen-containing medications. No central venous catheter, port, or peripherally inserted central line is present; today’s intravenous access is a single 20-gauge cannula in the left forearm placed by pre-op nursing staff. Review of extremities reveals a spray of dilated, tortuous superficial veins along the posterior calves and medial thighs that enlarge when the legs dangle; the skin is intact, warm, and of normal color, with symmetrical calf circumferences and no pitting, cords, or tenderness. He specifically notes that his lower legs never feel tight or appear puffier at the end of the day. Vital signs on arrival: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/74 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats/min and regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96 % on ambient air. Body mass index is 27 kg/m². He is conversational, oriented, and displays no acute distress. Jugular venous pulsation is within normal limits, carotid upstrokes are brisk, and the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced; S1 and S2 are crisp without gallop or pathologic murmurs. Lungs are clear to auscultation with scattered end-expiratory wheezes over the right upper lobe but no crackles. Abdomen is soft and nondistended, with normoactive bowel sounds and no hepatosplenomegaly. The right knee exhibits a positive McMurray click on valgus stress but no effusion; range of motion is limited by pain beyond 110 degrees of flexion. Distal pulses are 2+ bilaterally, capillary refill is rapid, and sensation is intact in all dermatomes. Neurologic examination shows 5/5 strength in upper and contralateral lower limbs, normal tone, and symmetric reflexes. Skin elsewhere is free of ulcers, petechiae, or ecchymoses; no palpable lymphadenopathy is appreciated. Pre-operative laboratory studies obtained yesterday reveal hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, hematocrit 42 %, platelet count 253 × 10⁹/L, white blood cells 7.0 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 20 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.1 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s. A 12-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 76 bpm without ST-segment deviation, and a chest radiograph obtained for pre-operative clearance demonstrates hyperinflated lungs without infiltrate or mass. Airway evaluation reveals Mallampati class II, full neck extension, and adequate mouth opening with no dental instability, suggesting straightforward intubation. He has been fasting since midnight, took his morning tiotropium inhalation, held all aspirin as directed, and consents to intraoperative pneumatic calf compression; pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis will be selected following formal risk assessment that accounts for his prior immune-mediated platelet reaction, chronic lung condition, visible superficial venous dilation, and the planned arthroscopic intervention of limited duration.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini surgical VTE risk score sums weighted patient and procedure factors present at preoperative assessment.
- Age 56 (41–60 years) = 1.
- BMI 27 kg/m² (>25) = 1.
- Visible tortuous varicose veins = 1. There is no leg edema to score separately.
- COPD (abnormal pulmonary function) = 1.
- Planned knee arthroscopy = 2. Count the arthroscopic procedure once, not also as minor surgery or joint replacement.
- Prior confirmed heparin-induced thrombocytopenia = 3, despite the currently normal platelet count.
No additional points are supported for prior VTE, immobility, malignancy, or central venous access.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 9.
Final answer: 9
